title: Two Slits
intro: Both slits are open, so the packet goes through both and interferes with itself. Bright fringes are where the two paths add; dark fringes are where they cancel. The mines sit near dark fringes. Faster packets spread less on the way, but the fringe pattern also fans out with time (spacing ≈ 2πt / slit separation), so watch where the dark bands are when you observe.
naiveSkip: introductory level: in 2D, slit diffraction spreads P_T thinly whatever you do; the Mach–Zehnder levels (3-2, 5-1) carry the interference lessons
goal: Choose the packet's speed and width, run it through the two slits, and observe when the fringes lie over the target. Keep clear of the two mines.

physics.point: The particle's wave goes through both slits. Where the two parts arrive half a wavelength out of step they cancel, leaving dark fringes where the particle is never found.

idea: Nothing here splits the particle into two halves. Its wave passes through both slits, and beyond the wall the two parts overlap. The chance of finding the particle is |ψ|², the square of their sum, not the sum of two separate chances.

Where the two waves arrive in step they add, and |ψ|² can reach four times what one slit gives alone: a bright fringe. Where one arrives half a wavelength behind the other they cancel: a dark fringe. Open both slits, and the particle stops landing in places that either slit alone would send it to.
The fringes are not fixed lines. The wave keeps spreading after the slits, so the pattern fans out as time passes and the dark bands drift away from the centre.
In two dimensions most of the probability never reaches the target. About 60% bounces off the wall, and what gets through spreads over a wide fan. That is why the star thresholds here are low.
maths: From two slits a distance d apart to a point at distance D and height y off the axis, the paths differ by about d·y/D. The phase difference is k times that:

maths.eq:
Δφ ≈ k·d·y / D
dark fringes where Δφ = π, 3π, …

maths: So neighbouring fringes are Δy = 2πD/(k·d) = λD/d apart. A packet of speed k covers D = k·t in the time t after the slits, so k cancels:

At a fixed time the spacing does not depend on k. A slower packet takes longer to reach the target, though, so its fringes are wider when they arrive there: at x = 32 (D ≈ 20) the formula gives Δy ≈ 7.9 for k = 2 and ≈ 5.6 for k = 2.8. The simulation shows 7.8 and 5.3.

The mines sit 4 above and below the centre. They lie on the first dark fringes when Δy ≈ 8, which the default k = 2 reaches around t ≈ 12.8. These estimates treat the slits as points and the packet as having one speed, so they are good to about 10%.
try: Keep the default k = 2 and σ = 2.8, and pause near t ≈ 12.8. The dark bands either side of the centre now lie on the mines, at y ≈ 16 and 24. Observing there gives P_T ≈ 9%.
Set k = 2.8 and σ = 3.5 and observe at t ≈ 9.2. The fringes are tighter (dark bands at y ≈ 17.3 and 22.7), and P_T ≈ 13%, the best this level offers.
Set k = 1.4. The packet arrives late (best moment t ≈ 17) and its fringes are wide, with the first dark bands near y ≈ 15 and 25.
